paragraphs.source_en: After the two of them had gone out, I helped myself without ceremony to the half slice of fish cake that Mr. Kangetsu had bitten and left behind. These days I am no longer an ordinary, commonplace cat. I feel that I have fully acquired the qualifications of the sort of cat described by Momokawa Joen, or perhaps of the cat that once stole goldfish from the Gray household. Blacky from the rickshaw man’s house is no longer worth my notice at all. Even if I were to dispose of a slice of fish cake, people would hardly have any right to grumble. Besides, this habit of snatching a snack when no one is watching is by no means limited to us cats. Take our maid Osan, for instance: whenever the mistress is out, she often helps herself to rice cakes and sweets without asking, and after eating them she says nothing about it either. Nor is Osan the only one; even the children whom the mistress is always praising as extremely well brought up show the same tendency. It happened four or five days ago: the two children woke very early, and before the master and his wife had risen, they sat facing each other at the dining table. Every day they are given some of the bread the master eats, with white sugar sprinkled on it. As it happened, the sugar jar was on the table that day, and even the sugar spoon was there. Since there was no one to divide out their sugar as usual, the elder child soon scooped a spoonful from the jar and poured it onto her own plate. Then the younger one, imitating her sister, scooped sugar onto her own plate in the same way. The two of them stared wide-eyed at one another for a while; then the elder took up the spoon again and added another spoonful to her plate. The younger immediately took the spoon as well and made the amount on her own plate equal to her sister’s. The elder sister scooped another spoonful, and the younger sister, not to be outdone, added another too. So it went on, one spoonful after another, until at last the sugar on both plates rose into little mountains and not a single spoonful was left in the jar. Just then the master came out of the bedroom rubbing his sleepy eyes, and put all the sugar the children had labored so hard to scoop back into the jar as before. Seeing this scene, I thought: the human notion of fairness, worked out from selfishness, may perhaps be superior to that of us cats, but in wisdom they seem far inferior to cats. Would it not have been better to get the sugar into their mouths quickly, before it piled up into little mountains? Unfortunately they cannot understand what I say, so to my regret I had no choice but to sit silently on the rice tub and watch this lively little drama unfold.

units.source_en: After the two of them had gone out, I helped myself without ceremony to the half slice of fish cake that Mr. Kangetsu had bitten and left behind.
units.source_zh: 两人出门以后，我不客气地把寒月君咬剩下的半片“鱼糕”给报销了。

units.source_en: These days I am no longer an ordinary, commonplace cat.
units.source_zh: 这些日子，我已不是普普通通的猫了。

units.source_en: I feel that I have fully acquired the qualifications of the sort of cat described by Momokawa Joen, or perhaps of the cat that once stole goldfish from the Gray household.
units.source_zh: 我觉得自己已完全获得了像桃山如燕所描述的那种猫儿的资格，或者说像格雷家偷过金鱼的那只猫儿的资格啦。

units.source_en: Blacky from the rickshaw man’s house is no longer worth my notice at all.
units.source_zh: 车夫家的老黑已根本不在我的眼里了。

units.source_en: Even if I were to dispose of a slice of fish cake, people would hardly have any right to grumble.
units.source_zh: 即便报销了一片“鱼糕”，人们也不会说三道四。

units.source_en: Besides, this habit of snatching a snack when no one is watching is by no means limited to us cats.
units.source_zh: 而且这种利用别人看不见的当儿偷吃零食的习惯，也决不限于我们猫族。

units.source_en: Take our maid Osan, for instance: whenever the mistress is out, she often helps herself to rice cakes and sweets without asking, and after eating them she says nothing about it either.
units.source_zh: 就拿我家女仆阿三说吧，她趁主人妻子不在的时候，经常不打招呼就吃点心之类的东西，而且吃完了也不打招呼。

units.source_en: Nor is Osan the only one; even the children whom the mistress is always praising as extremely well brought up show the same tendency.
units.source_zh: 这种事也不只限于阿三，就连一向被主人妻子吹嘘为有极好家教的孩子们，也有类似行为。

units.source_en: It happened four or five days ago: the two children woke very early, and before the master and his wife had risen, they sat facing each other at the dining table.
units.source_zh: 这是四五天前的事了：两个孩子清早醒来，在主人夫妇还未起床之前，便面对面地坐在饭桌上。

units.source_en: Every day they are given some of the bread the master eats, with white sugar sprinkled on it.
units.source_zh: 她们每天总是要吃一点主人吃的那种蘸白糖的面包。

units.source_en: As it happened, the sugar jar was on the table that day, and even the sugar spoon was there.
units.source_zh: 碰巧那天糖罐正好放在桌上，并且连糖匙也在。

units.source_en: Since there was no one to divide out their sugar as usual, the elder child soon scooped a spoonful from the jar and poured it onto her own plate.

ja.t: してくれるものがないので、

units.source_zh: 因为没有人像平常那样给她们分白糖，那个大点的孩子很快从糖罐里用糖匙舀了一匙糖，倒在自己的碟子里。

units.source_en: Then the younger one, imitating her sister, scooped sugar onto her own plate in the same way.
units.source_zh: 于是那个小的，也学着姐姐的样子，用同样的办法把糖舀在自己的碟子里。

units.source_en: The two of them stared wide-eyed at one another for a while; then the elder took up the spoon again and added another spoonful to her plate.
units.source_zh: 两个人睁圆眼睛对视了一会儿，那个大的，又拿起糖匙舀了一匙加在自己的碟子里。

units.source_en: The younger immediately took the spoon as well and made the amount on her own plate equal to her sister’s.
units.source_zh: 那个小的也立刻拿过糖匙，把自己的碟子弄成和姐姐的一样多。

units.source_en: The elder sister scooped another spoonful, and the younger sister, not to be outdone, added another too.
units.source_zh: 姐姐又舀了一匙，妹妹也不落后，又加上了一匙。

units.source_en: So it went on, one spoonful after another, until at last the sugar on both plates rose into little mountains and not a single spoonful was left in the jar.

ja.t: っておらんようになった。

units.source_zh: 这样你一匙我一匙舀下去，终于两人碟子里的糖都堆成了小山，而罐子里连一匙糖也不剩了。

units.source_en: Just then the master came out of the bedroom rubbing his sleepy eyes, and put all the sugar the children had labored so hard to scoop back into the jar as before.
units.source_zh: 这时，主人揉着惺忪的睡眼从寝室走了出来，把孩子们费了好大力气舀出来的糖又照旧装回罐子里。

units.source_en: Seeing this scene, I thought: the human notion of fairness, worked out from selfishness, may perhaps be superior to that of us cats, but in wisdom they seem far inferior to cats.
units.source_zh: 我看到这种光景，心想：“人类从利己主义引申出来的所谓公平观念，也许优于我们猫族，不过他们的智慧似乎比我们猫儿差远了。

ja.t: めてしまえばいいにと

units.source_zh: 在糖没有堆成小山之前，赶快把它送入嘴里岂不更好吗？”

units.source_en: Unfortunately they cannot understand what I say, so to my regret I had no choice but to sit silently on the rice tub and watch this lively little drama unfold.
units.source_zh: 可惜我说的话她们听不懂，所以很遗憾，我只好坐在盛饭的桶上默不作声地欣赏着这幕活剧。

paragraphs.source_zh: 两人出门以后，我不客气地把寒月君咬剩下的半片“鱼糕”给报销了。这些日子，我已不是普普通通的猫了。我觉得自己已完全获得了像桃山如燕所描述的那种猫儿的资格，或者说像格雷家偷过金鱼的那只猫儿的资格啦。车夫家的老黑已根本不在我的眼里了。即便报销了一片“鱼糕”，人们也不会说三道四。而且这种利用别人看不见的当儿偷吃零食的习惯，也决不限于我们猫族。就拿我家女仆阿三说吧，她趁主人妻子不在的时候，经常不打招呼就吃点心之类的东西，而且吃完了也不打招呼。这种事也不只限于阿三，就连一向被主人妻子吹嘘为有极好家教的孩子们，也有类似行为。这是四五天前的事了：两个孩子清早醒来，在主人夫妇还未起床之前，便面对面地坐在饭桌上。她们每天总是要吃一点主人吃的那种蘸白糖的面包。碰巧那天糖罐正好放在桌上，并且连糖匙也在。因为没有人像平常那样给她们分白糖，那个大点的孩子很快从糖罐里用糖匙舀了一匙糖，倒在自己的碟子里。于是那个小的，也学着姐姐的样子，用同样的办法把糖舀在自己的碟子里。两个人睁圆眼睛对视了一会儿，那个大的，又拿起糖匙舀了一匙加在自己的碟子里。那个小的也立刻拿过糖匙，把自己的碟子弄成和姐姐的一样多。姐姐又舀了一匙，妹妹也不落后，又加上了一匙。这样你一匙我一匙舀下去，终于两人碟子里的糖都堆成了小山，而罐子里连一匙糖也不剩了。这时，主人揉着惺忪的睡眼从寝室走了出来，把孩子们费了好大力气舀出来的糖又照旧装回罐子里。我看到这种光景，心想：“人类从利己主义引申出来的所谓公平观念，也许优于我们猫族，不过他们的智慧似乎比我们猫儿差远了。在糖没有堆成小山之前，赶快把它送入嘴里岂不更好吗？”可惜我说的话她们听不懂，所以很遗憾，我只好坐在盛饭的桶上默不作声地欣赏着这幕活剧。
